A five-step AI research workflow: frame the question, collect sources, extract with citations, synthesise, then verify the load-bearing claims.

Most AI research fails in a predictable way: you ask a question, receive a fluent answer, and three weeks later discover that none of it could be traced to a source anyone else can open. The problem is rarely the model. It is that ask, read and accept is not a workflow — it is a habit, and habits collapse as soon as a deadline appears.

What follows is a five-step routine that works on almost any research task, from a competitor review to a literature scan. It is deliberately tool-agnostic, because the steps that prevent errors are procedural rather than technical: nothing here depends on which assistant you use.

Step 1: Frame the question before you open a chatbot

Write down the question you are actually trying to answer, in one sentence, plus the decision it feeds. Research without a decision attached has no stopping rule, and a workflow without a stopping rule turns into an afternoon of open tabs. A useful frame has three parts:

  • The question — specific enough that a wrong answer would be obvious to you.
  • The decision — what you will do differently once you know the answer.
  • The bar — what counts as adequate evidence: one primary source, three independent confirmations, a named dataset.

Put that frame at the top of your prompt. A model asked "I am deciding whether to move our documentation into a new help centre; I need to know what actually drives self-serve support rates" will answer something usable. The same model asked "tell me about customer support" will produce something you can only read.

Step 2: Collect candidates, then open the originals

Use an answer engine or an assistant to gather candidate sources quickly, because this is where AI is genuinely faster than manual search. Then break the habit that causes most research failures: citing the answer instead of the source. Open the page the model referenced and confirm three things — the claim is actually there, it says what the summary says it says, and the page is the version you think it is. Studies get revised, press releases get updated, articles get corrected.

Keep a simple source table as you go: address, what it claims, date, and whether you have opened it yourself. Anything you have not opened is a rumour with a hyperlink. Where answer engines are strong and where they still mislead, we worked through the evidence in our Perplexity vs Google Search comparison.

Two sources are not two if they copy each other. When two pages carry the same wording, the same figure and no independent citation behind them, treat them as one source and keep looking. Independence is the property you are collecting, not the number of open tabs.

Step 3: Extract in passes, keeping citations attached

Do not ask for a summary of everything in a single request. Long documents and mixed sources degrade when a model compresses them together, because the second source is quietly filtered through the first. Work in two passes instead: extract claims and figures from each source individually, with a quote or location attached to each item, then compare those extractions across sources and flag the disagreements.

The rule that makes this work is simple — no claim without a location. If a figure cannot be traced back to where it came from within a few seconds, it does not enter your notes. That one rule removes the most common way confident research becomes wrong: a number that was accurate in one context being reused in another.

What it means for you: your notes should be auditable by someone who was not in the room. If a colleague cannot find where a claim came from without asking you, the workflow is unfinished — however good the summary reads.

Step 4: Synthesise into your own structure

With clean extractions, do the thinking yourself, using the model as a sparring partner rather than as the author. Ask it to attack your outline: what is missing, what is contradicted, which point is really two points in disguise. Then settle the structure — headings, order, argument — before any prose exists.

Most people do this backwards. They ask for a draft first and try to edit it into shape, which means they inherit the model's structure, and the model's structure is always the average structure. For prompts at this stage, the five-slot prompt framework gives you a repeatable format.

What it means for you: the outline you argue about is the research. If you cannot defend the order of your sections out loud, you do not yet understand the material, and no amount of drafting will repair that.

Step 5: Verify the load-bearing claims

You cannot check everything, so check what the conclusion rests on. List the three or four claims that would collapse your finding if they turned out to be wrong, and verify each against a primary source: the original study, the official documentation, the filing, the dataset. Everything else can carry a lighter check.

Two patterns survive every model release. The first is plausible specificity — a statistic with decimal places and a year attached reads as verified even when it was invented. The second is source drift, where a real source is described accurately but supports a narrower claim than the one being made. Our fact-checking routine covers both in about the time it takes to read this article.

Common mistakes, and a checklist

The workflow above is short enough to remember. Most breakdowns come from one of five predictable shortcuts:

  1. Starting with the model instead of the question. If you cannot state the decision, you cannot judge the answer.
  2. Citing the summary. An answer engine is a routing layer, not a source.
  3. Batch-compressing everything at once. Per-source passes keep figures attached to their context.
  4. Letting the model choose your structure. Average outlines produce average documents.
  5. Verifying only the conclusion. Check the claims underneath it, or the conclusion is decoration.

Before you file anything, run the short version: every number has a location, every source has been opened, the load-bearing claims have primary confirmation, and the structure is one you could defend without the notes in front of you. If all four hold, the work will still be defensible in six months, which is more than most AI-assisted research manages.

Frequently asked questions

How long does an AI research workflow take?

For a medium question, expect a short framing session, a source-collection pass, and one focused extraction pass per document. Verifying the load-bearing claims is usually the quickest stage. In practice the routine saves time rather than adding it, because you stop re-reading material you have already processed and stop chasing sources you never opened.

Do I need a paid AI tool for research?

Not to start. Free tiers handle framing, extraction and drafting well enough for occasional work. Paid plans matter when you process long documents regularly, need higher usage limits, or rely on features such as project workspaces and file uploads. Upgrade when a limit interrupts you more than twice in a week, not before.

How do I stop AI inventing sources?

Treat every reference as a claim to be checked. Ask the model to quote the exact sentence and give its location, then open the original and confirm the sentence exists and supports the point. Record nothing you have not opened yourself. That takes seconds per source and removes the most common way AI-assisted research goes wrong.
